nameStory: Sulphur cinquefoil gets its name from its bright sulfur-yellow flowers that bloom throughout summer. The word 'cinquefoil' comes from French meaning 'five leaves,' referring to the plant's characteristic hand-shaped leaves with five leaflets. It's like nature's own little yellow stars scattered across fields and roadsides.
description: Sulphur cinquefoil is a sturdy perennial wildflower that stands 1-3 feet tall with hairy, upright stems. It produces clusters of bright yellow, five-petaled flowers from late spring through summer that look like tiny buttercups. The distinctive hand-shaped leaves have five narrow, toothed leaflets that spread out like fingers. Originally from Europe and Asia, this hardy plant has made itself at home across New England's disturbed soils and open spaces.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright sulfur-yellow flowers with five rounded petals arranged in loose, flat-topped clusters at stem tips. Each flower is about half an inch across with a small green center, blooming from June through August.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Distinctive hand-shaped leaves with exactly five narrow, deeply-toothed leaflets that feel rough and hairy to the touch. The leaflets radiate out from a central point like fingers on a hand.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright, branching stems that feel noticeably hairy and rough when you run your hand along them. Plants form clumps 1-3 feet tall and can spread to create patches.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, dry, wrinkled seeds develop in late summer where flowers once bloomed. The seeds have a distinctly rough, bumpy texture that gives this species its alternate name 'rough-fruited cinquefoil.'

habitat: Look for sulphur cinquefoil in disturbed, sunny areas like roadsides, old fields, vacant lots, and pasture edges throughout New England. It thrives in poor, dry soils where other plants struggle and is often found along gravel shoulders and in areas with frequent soil disturbance. This tough plant tolerates drought and compacted soils, making it common around human activity.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge as fuzzy, five-fingered rosettes close to the ground. Plants begin growing upright stems with the distinctive hairy texture becoming noticeable.
seasonality.summer: Peak identification time with bright yellow flower clusters blooming from June through August. The rough, hairy stems and hand-shaped leaves are fully developed and easy to spot.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and rough seeds develop. Leaves may turn yellowish before dying back, and dried seed heads persist on brown stems.
seasonality.winter: Plants die back to ground level, leaving only dried stems and seed heads. Look for dead rosettes of the distinctive five-fingered leaves.

funFact: Despite being called a 'minor noxious weed' in some areas, sulphur cinquefoil was actually one of the ingredients in medieval 'flying ointments' that witches supposedly used - though the only thing that would fly were the imaginations of those who applied these herbal concoctions!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with wild strawberry, but sulphur cinquefoil has yellow flowers (not white) and five leaflets per leaf instead of three. Remember: 'Five fingers, yellow singers' for sulphur cinquefoil versus 'three leaves, white please' for wild strawberry.
contextualKnowledge: This European immigrant arrived in North America in the 1800s and has proven remarkably adaptable to disturbed habitats. While some areas consider it weedy, it's actually quite beneficial for pollinators during the summer bloom period when many native flowers have finished.
compareHints: Sulphur cinquefoil stands out from other New England cinquefoils primarily by its bright yellow flowers and consistently five-fingered leaves. Silvery cinquefoil has similar yellow flowers but silvery-white leaf undersides, while dwarf and common cinquefoils are much smaller, creeping plants. The upright, hairy growth habit and robust size make sulphur cinquefoil the most noticeable of the yellow-flowered cinquefoils.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's cinquefoils, silvery cinquefoil is the only one with dramatically silver-white fuzzy leaf undersides - dwarf and common cinquefoil have plain green undersides, while rough cinquefoil has much larger, coarsely-toothed leaves.
Among New England's cinquefoils, dwarf cinquefoil is distinguished by its truly prostrate, mat-forming habit with rooting runners.
Common cinquefoil differs from dwarf cinquefoil by its longer, more obvious runners and slightly larger flowers.
Unlike other cinquefoils in its genus which typically have five-part leaves (the name cinquefoil means 'five leaves'), mock strawberry has three-part leaves like true strawberries.
Unlike most other New England cinquefoils which have five leaflets, rough cinquefoil stands out with just three leaflets per leaf.
Lesser mock-strawberry differs from other cinquefoils by having three-part leaves instead of the typical five-part leaves (cinque means five in French).
Unlike its lowland cinquefoil relatives that spread by runners or grow as larger plants, dwarf mountain cinquefoil forms tiny, tight cushions and never leaves the alpine zone.

Among New England's cinquefoils, creeping cinquefoil is unique for its long trailing runners and five-leaflet leaves – most other cinquefoils like common cinquefoil and dwarf cinquefoil have three leaflets and don't spread by runners.

Intermediate cinquefoil differs from common New England cinquefoils like dwarf cinquefoil by its specific leaflet count and arrangement, and from sulphur cinquefoil by its smaller stature and different leaf texture.
Unlike its inland cinquefoil relatives, coast cinquefoil has adapted specifically to maritime conditions with its more compact, mat-forming growth and thicker, more succulent-like leaves.
